sections.h2: Where is Gallatin, Tennessee, and how did it start?
sections.html:
The Cumberland River runs past Gallatin, which serves as Sumner County's seat and lies roughly 30 miles northeast of Nashville. Settlers secured the land along Station Camp Creek early, and Captain William Asher built a fortified station there in 1780. The town was established in 1802 and named for Albert Gallatin, the Treasury Secretary under Jefferson and Madison. Andrew Jackson bought one of the first lots after the 1803 survey, and the town incorporated in 1815.

The Union Army took the town in February 1862 because of its railroad and river position, and Union troops occupied it for the rest of the war. A cholera epidemic hit in the summer of 1873. The calendar includes the Sumner County Fair in the last week of August, a Fall Festival on the square, a Christmas parade and a Candlelight Cemetery Tour on the first Saturday of October. The Palace, a single-screen theater from 1908, has been restored. Historic buildings that survive include Cragfont, Rosemont and Trousdale Place, and the city has a central historic district.

Gallatin has grown quickly. The Census Bureau counted 30,278 people in 2010 and 44,431 in 2020, and its July 2025 estimate is 54,590, a 22.8 percent jump from the 2020 base. Land area is 32.17 square miles.

That pace of growth is the background to the new zoning ordinance the city adopted in 2026, covered below, and to the Station Camp and Liberty Creek school campuses on the list further down.

sections.h2: Which employers keep Gallatin's housing market moving?
sections.html:
Gallatin's largest named employers and projects include:

  • Gap, Inc., with 1,250 workers, plus Sumner Regional Medical Center (now Highpoint Health), Volunteer State Community College and RR Donnelley
  • Beretta, the Italian gunmaker, which moved its US production here in 2015
  • Meta, whose data center of more than 1.6 million square feet opened in 2020, with a 2024 expansion announced to lift its Gallatin investment past $1 billion
  • The Tennessee Valley Authority, which operates a coal-fired power plant in the city

Highpoint Health, the former Sumner Regional Medical Center, operates an emergency room, a cancer program, a wound care center and a cardiac catheterization lab. Vol State, part of the Tennessee Board of Regents system, has its main campus in Gallatin and has drawn more than 150,000 students since 1971. Sumner County's unemployment rate was 2.8 percent in March 2025.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about houses in Gallatin?
sections.html:
QuickFacts lists a $372,000 median value for Gallatin's owned homes in the 2020 to 2024 survey, above the national $332,700 and well below Franklin's $705,400. Monthly costs for owners are $1,778 with a loan and $552 without. Rent has a median of $1,395. Among 19,755 households, 57.1 percent own.

The household income median is $77,518, the poverty rate is 13.0 percent, and 33.5 percent of people past 25 hold a bachelor's degree.

sections.h2: Which roads and schools matter to Gallatin buyers?
sections.html:
US 31E, also called Nashville Pike or Gallatin Road, is the main street through town. State Route 386, Vietnam Veterans Boulevard, is a controlled-access road that ends in Gallatin and links to Interstate 65. State Routes 109 and 25 complete the network, and WeGo Public Transit runs a daily bus to downtown Nashville. Sumner County Regional Airport has a 5,000-foot runway.

The Sumner County Board of Education runs Gallatin's public schools, and these campuses serve the city:

  • High schools: Gallatin High, Station Camp High and Liberty Creek High
  • Middle schools: Joe Shafer, Liberty Creek, Station Camp and Rucker-Stewart
  • Elementary schools: Benny Bills, Guild, Howard, Liberty Creek, Station Camp, Union STEM and Vena Stuart

The county system had about 29,400 students in 49 schools as of August 2020. Old Hickory Lake and six city parks add recreation, including Lock 4, Triple Creek and Thompson parks.

sections.h2: How are Gallatin property taxes set and paid?
sections.html:
For 2026 the city charges $0.5295 on each $100 of assessed value, using values from the Sumner County assessor. Payment is due before March 1, when interest begins. Tennessee law does not require mailed notices, so an unreceived bill is no defense. Payment plans can be arranged through the Recorder's Office.

The city offers relief for qualifying elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners and disabled veteran or widow homeowners, and a tax freeze program that must be recertified every year through the Sumner County Trustee.

Sumner County reappraises every five years. The last reappraisal was 2024 and the next is scheduled for 2029. An owner who disputes a value begins with an informal review at the assessor's office. The next step is the county Board of Equalization, in session from June 1. Beyond that sits the State Board, with a deadline of August 1 or 45 days after the local notice, whichever falls later.

sections.h2: What do permits and the new zoning rules mean for a Gallatin seller?
sections.html:
Gallatin adopted a new zoning ordinance and zoning map effective September 1, 2026, so older notes on a lot's zoning may be out of date. The Planning Department also handles fences, signs, temporary use permits and flood zone questions. Its commission and zoning appeals board work on a six-week review cycle.

Building permits are applied for through the city's Citizens Self-Service Portal. Contractors must email permits@gallatintn.gov a copy of their state license, general liability and workers' compensation insurance or a state exemption, and a signed city permit bond with a power of attorney before they can apply.

If a past owner finished a basement or added a room, ask the city permit office at permits@gallatintn.gov whether permits were closed. A buyer's lender and inspector will ask the same question.

sections.h2: How is a Gallatin deed recorded?
sections.html:
Deeds for Gallatin houses go to the Sumner County Register of Deeds on North Belvedere Drive. Weekday hours are 8 to 4:30, and a typical year brings in more than 30,000 recorded documents. It accepts electronic filing through Simplifile and CSC, and it offers a free MyLandAlert notice that emails an owner when a document is recorded under their name.

The register collects the state conveyance tax, set by Revenue at 37 cents per $100 of price and owed by the grantee. Records are certified back to September 1989 and can be searched online, and deed books and indexes have been digitized back to 1786.

An heir or a seller in a hurry should have a title company confirm the chain of recorded deeds before a closing date is set.

faqs.a: About 54,590 as of July 2025, per the Census Bureau, compared with 44,431 counted in 2020, a rise of 22.8 percent over the estimates base.

faqs.q: What is the City of Gallatin property tax rate?
faqs.a: It is $0.5295 on each $100 of assessed value for 2026. Interest starts March 1 on anything unpaid.

faqs.q: When did Gallatin's new zoning ordinance take effect?
faqs.a: The city adopted a new zoning ordinance and zoning map as of September 1, 2026. Call the Planning Department at 615-451-5796 to confirm how a specific lot is zoned.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Sumner County property value?
faqs.a: Call the assessor at 615-452-2412 and request an informal review. If the value still looks wrong, file with the county Board of Equalization, which sits from June 1.

faqs.q: Which office files the deed on a Gallatin house?
faqs.a: The Sumner County Register of Deeds, Suite 201 at 355 N. Belvedere Dr. Call 615-452-3892. E-recording runs through Simplifile and CSC.
